title: The Book of Isaiah Timeline
sub: A Lawsuit Against Judah · Comfort, a Suffering Servant, and a New Creation
desc: Sixty-six chapters move from a courtroom indictment of Jerusalem through oracles against the nations and a historical interlude with Hezekiah, into the sweeping comfort, exile-ending prophecy, and Suffering Servant of chapters 40-66, closing on new heavens and a new earth.

eras.label: Era I · Isaiah 1
eras.name: The Lawsuit Against Judah and Jerusalem
eras.dates: The book opens not with narrative but with a courtroom scene: the LORD summons heaven and earth as witnesses against a rebellious people whose religious ritual has become a substitute for justice, closing with a promise that Zion will be refined rather than simply destroyed.

events.title: Superscription, and a Remnant Like Sodom Spared
events.detail: The book names its author, its royal timespan, and its subject in a single verse, then opens with the LORD's own lawsuit — an ox knows its owner better than Israel knows its God — before noting that only divine restraint kept the nation from complete annihilation like Sodom and Gomorrah.

verses.text: Listen, O heavens, pay attention, O earth! For the LORD [Yahweh] speaks: "I raised children, I brought them up, but they have rebelled against me! An ox recognizes its owner, a donkey recognizes where its owner puts its food; but Israel does not recognize me, my people do not understand."

events.title: "What Are Your Many Sacrifices to Me?"
events.detail: The LORD declares he is sick of Judah's festivals, sacrifices, and prayers, since their hands are stained with blood — but the chapter turns on a genuine offer: sins as scarlet can become white as snow if the nation will actually learn to do right.

verses.text: Wash! Cleanse yourselves! Remove your sinful deeds from my sight. Stop sinning. Learn to do what is right… "Come, let's consider your options," says the LORD [Yahweh]. "Though your sins have stained you like the color red, you can become white like snow."

events.title: Zion's Corruption, and a Refining Judgment
events.detail: The once-faithful city is now called a prostitute run by bribe-taking officials, and the LORD promises to "purify your metal with flux" — judgment aimed not merely at destruction but at restoring honest judges as in former days.

verses.text: I will attack you; I will purify your metal with flux. I will remove all your slag. I will reestablish honest judges as in former times… Then you will be called, 'The Just City, Faithful Town.'

eras.label: Era II · Isaiah 2
eras.name: The Mountain of the LORD's House, and the Day of Pride Humbled
eras.dates: A vision of a distant future when Zion becomes the world's center of instruction and war itself is obsolete opens the chapter, before it pivots hard into the present — a land full of idols, wealth, and horses that will all be humiliated on "the LORD's day" of judgment against everything proud and lofty.

events.title: "They Will Beat Their Swords Into Plowshares"
events.detail: In future days, all nations will stream to the LORD's mountain to learn his ways, and he will settle disputes between them so completely that swords become farm tools and war is no longer even practiced.

verses.text: They will beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks. Nations will not take up the sword against other nations, and they will no longer train for war.

events.title: "The LORD Alone Will Be Exalted in That Day"
events.detail: A land full of foreign diviners, silver, horses, and idols is warned that a day of judgment is coming against everything high and proud — mountains, towers, ships — until people throw their own silver and gold idols into caves and stop trusting in mere human breath.

verses.text: Proud men will be brought low, arrogant men will be humiliated; the LORD [Yahweh] alone will be exalted in that day.
Stop trusting in human beings, whose life's breath is in their nostrils. For why should they be given special consideration?

eras.label: Era III · Isaiah 3-4
eras.name: Jerusalem's Leaders Stripped, and a Purified Remnant
eras.dates: Every source of social stability — warriors, judges, advisers — is removed from Jerusalem in a cascade of collapsing leadership, Zion's proud women are stripped of their jewelry down to rope and branding, and the chapter closes on the far side of judgment, with a remnant made holy under a canopy of cloud and fire.

events.title: Every Source of Security Removed
events.detail: The LORD strips Jerusalem of its warriors, judges, and skilled advisers alike, leaving youths and "riffraff" to rule — a society-wide collapse blamed directly on leaders who have "stashed in your houses what you have stolen from the poor."

verses.text: The LORD comes to pronounce judgment on the leaders of his people… "It is you who have ruined the vineyard! You have stashed in your houses what you have stolen from the poor. Why do you crush my people and grind the faces of the poor?"

events.title: Zion's Daughters Stripped of Their Finery
events.detail: In one of the book's most vivid catalogs, a long list of jewelry, veils, and fine robes worn by Zion's proud, flirtatious women is itemized only to be stripped away, replaced by baldness, sackcloth, and a slave's branding.

verses.text: A putrid stench will replace the smell of spices, a rope will replace a belt, baldness will replace braided locks of hair, a sackcloth garment will replace a fine robe, and a prisoner's brand will replace beauty.

events.title: A Purified Remnant Under the LORD's Canopy
events.detail: On the far side of judgment, those "destined to live" in Jerusalem are called holy, and the LORD himself becomes a canopy of cloud by day and fire by night over Mount Zion — deliberately recalling the wilderness pillar that once led Israel out of Egypt.

verses.text: Then the LORD [Yahweh] will create over all Mount Zion… a cloud and smoke by day and a bright flame of fire by night; indeed a canopy will accompany the LORD's [Yahweh's] glorious presence.

eras.label: Era IV · Isaiah 5
eras.name: The Song of the Vineyard, and Six Woes
eras.dates: Isaiah sings a love song about a carefully tended vineyard that produced only sour grapes — a parable that turns out to be Israel itself — before pronouncing a rhythmic series of "beware" oracles against greed, drunkenness, and moral inversion, and ending on the image of a foreign army summoned from the ends of the earth.

events.title: The Song of the Vineyard
events.detail: Isaiah sings as if for a friend about a vineyard cleared of stones, planted with the best vines, and fitted with a watchtower and winepress — only to produce worthless fruit, and the song turns at its final line to reveal the vineyard is "the people of Judah" themselves.

verses.text: Indeed, Israel is the vineyard of the LORD [Yahweh] of Heaven's Armies, the people of Judah are the cultivated place in which he took delight. He waited for justice, but look what he got—disobedience!

events.title: Six "Beware" Oracles
events.detail: A rhythmic series of woes targets those who buy up all the land, drink from morning until night, call evil good and good evil, and pronounce the guilty innocent for a bribe — a catalog of exactly the moral inversions the vineyard song implied.

verses.text: Beware, those who call evil good and good evil, who turn darkness into light and light into darkness, who turn bitter into sweet and sweet into bitter.

events.title: A Distant Nation Summoned
events.detail: The chapter closes with fire consuming dry grass as a picture of coming judgment, then pivots to an actual invading army — tireless, sharp-arrowed, lion-voiced — summoned from far away with nothing standing in its way.

eras.label: Era V · Isaiah 6
eras.name: Isaiah's Call and Commission
eras.dates: In the year King Uzziah died, Isaiah sees the LORD himself seated on a high throne surrounded by six-winged seraphs — a vision that first devastates him with his own uncleanness, then cleanses him with a burning coal, before commissioning him to a uniquely difficult task: preaching to a people who will not understand no matter how clearly he speaks.

events.title: "Holy, Holy, Holy" — the Vision, and the Burning Coal
events.detail: Isaiah sees the LORD seated on a high throne, his robe filling the temple, while seraphs cry "holy, holy, holy" until the doorframes shake — a vision that leaves the prophet certain of his own doom, until a seraph touches his lips with a coal from the altar and declares his sin forgiven.

verses.text: "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD [Yahweh] of Heaven's Armies! His majestic splendor fills the entire earth!"… I said, "Woe to me! I am destroyed, for my lips are contaminated by sin."

events.title: "Here I Am, Send Me" — and the Hardening Commission
events.detail: Isaiah volunteers eagerly for a commission that turns out to be strange and severe — preaching in a way that will make the people's hearts even more calloused — and asks how long this will last, receiving an answer that reaches all the way to cities in ruins and a remnant reduced to a tenth.

verses.text: "Go and tell these people: 'Listen continually, but don't understand… make their ears deaf and their eyes blind.'" I replied, "How long, Lord [Adonai]?" He said, "Until cities are in ruins and unpopulated."

eras.label: Era VI · Isaiah 7
eras.name: The Sign of Immanuel
eras.dates: As two enemy kings march on Jerusalem, the LORD sends Isaiah to tell a terrified King Ahaz to stay calm and trust him — and when Ahaz refuses even to ask for a confirming sign, the LORD gives one anyway, promising a child named Immanuel whose early childhood will outlast the threat entirely, before the chapter closes on the devastation Assyria will bring instead.

events.title: "Don't Be Intimidated by These Two Stubs of Smoking Logs"
events.detail: With Syria and Israel allied against Jerusalem, the LORD sends Isaiah and his son Shear Jashub to meet the shaken King Ahaz with a message of calm — the two attacking kings are nothing more than smoking embers about to go out.

verses.text: "Ephraim's leader is Samaria, and Samaria's leader is the son of Remaliah. If your faith does not remain firm, then you will not remain secure."

events.title: The Sign of Immanuel
events.detail: When Ahaz refuses to ask for a sign, claiming piety, the LORD gives one regardless — a young woman will conceive and bear a son named Immanuel, "God with us," and before the child is old enough to know right from wrong, the land of Ahaz's two enemy kings will be desolate.

verses.text: "Therefore the Lord [Adonai] himself will give you a confirming sign. Look, this young woman is about to conceive and will give birth to a son. You, young woman, will name him Immanuel."

events.title: The Coming Assyrian Razor
events.detail: The relief promised in the sign has a cost attached: the LORD will use the king of Assyria "like a razor" against Ahaz's own land, turning once-cultivated hillsides into thornbush country grazed over by cattle and sheep.

eras.label: Era VII · Isaiah 8
eras.name: Maher-Shalal-Hash-Baz, and the Stone of Stumbling
eras.dates: Isaiah names his newborn son with a message of imminent Assyrian plunder, then describes that same Assyrian flood overtaking Judah itself — closing with the LORD offered as either a sanctuary or a stone people trip over, and a call to trust prophetic revelation over necromancy.

events.title: "Maher Shalal Hash Baz", and "God Is With Us"
events.detail: Isaiah's own son is named "Quick to the plunder, swift to the spoil" as a living countdown to Damascus and Samaria's fall, and the chapter pictures Assyria as a flood that will reach Judah's very neck — checked only by the recurring assurance that "God is with us."

verses.text: "Devise your strategy, but it will be thwarted. Issue your orders, but they will not be executed! For God is with us!"

events.title: The LORD as Sanctuary and Stumbling Stone
events.detail: The LORD warns Isaiah not to fear what the people fear, since he himself will become either a sanctuary or a trap depending on how he is received — a warning against consulting the dead for guidance instead of the LORD's own instruction, closing on a note of gloom that the next chapter immediately answers. NET's own text marks the underlying Hebrew chapter boundary here at 9:1, one verse later than most English Bibles number it.

verses.text: "You must recognize the authority of the LORD [Yahweh] of Heaven's Armies. He is the one you must respect; he is the one you must fear." He will become a sanctuary, but a stone that makes a person trip and a rock that makes one stumble.

eras.label: Era VIII · Isaiah 9
eras.name: Unto Us a Child Is Born, and Judgment on Israel's Pride
eras.dates: One of the book's most familiar passages — a royal child given titles like "Mighty God" and "Prince of Peace" — opens the chapter with light breaking into darkness, before it turns to judgment on Israel's arrogant self-confidence, repeating a grim refrain four times: "his anger does not subside, and his hand is ready to strike again." This chapter is numbered one verse earlier in most English Bibles, since NET's own text marks the underlying Hebrew boundary at what it calls 8:23/9:1.

events.title: "Unto Us a Child Is Born"
events.detail: Light dawns on a people who walked in darkness, and a child is given titles no ordinary heir could carry — Wonderful Adviser, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace — reigning on David's throne with justice that has no end. (Numbered 9:2-8 in most English translations.)

verses.text: For a child has been born to us, a son has been given to us. He shoulders responsibility and is called Wonderful Adviser, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.

events.title: "His Hand Is Ready to Strike Again"
events.detail: Israel's arrogant, self-rebuilding confidence after disaster only provokes further judgment, driving the LORD to "cut off Israel's head and tail" through a refrain repeated four times across the chapter that his anger has not yet subsided. (Numbered 9:9-21 in most English translations.)

verses.text: "The bricks have fallen, but we will rebuild with chiseled stone; the sycamore fig trees have been cut down, but we will replace them with cedars."

eras.label: Era IX · Isaiah 10
eras.name: Woe to Assyria, the Rod of God's Anger
eras.dates: Unjust lawmakers who exploit widows and orphans are condemned first, before the chapter turns to Assyria itself — used deliberately by the LORD as a disciplining rod, yet arrogant enough to think its conquests were its own achievement, and therefore due for judgment in turn once it has served its purpose.

events.title: Woe to Unjust Legislators
events.detail: A brief but pointed woe targets those who write oppressive laws specifically to deprive widows and orphans of justice, warning they will have nowhere to run on the day of reckoning.

events.title: Assyria, the Rod of the LORD's Anger — Then Judged for Its Pride
events.detail: Assyria is named outright as the club the LORD uses to punish a godless nation, but Assyria's own goal is conquest for its own sake — boasting that it gathered the earth's wealth "as one gathers up abandoned eggs" — so the LORD promises that once the rod has done its work, it will be broken in turn for its arrogance.

verses.text: Does an ax exalt itself over the one who wields it or a saw magnify itself over the one who cuts with it?

events.title: A Remnant Will Return
events.detail: Israel is promised it will finally stop leaning on the very foreign power that oppressed it and rely on the LORD instead, while Assyria's own advancing army is tracked town by town toward Jerusalem before being pictured as a forest chopped down to nothing.

verses.text: At that time those left in Israel… will no longer rely on a foreign leader that abuses them. Instead they will truly rely on the LORD [Yahweh], the Holy One of Israel. A remnant will come back, a remnant of Jacob, to the mighty God [El].

eras.label: Era X · Isaiah 11-12
eras.name: The Root of Jesse, and a Song of Deliverance
eras.dates: A royal figure described as a shoot from Jesse's own root stock will govern with perfect justice in a renewed creation where predator and prey lie down together, gathering Israel's scattered remnant home from every direction — a vision so complete it closes not in narrative but in song.

events.title: A Shoot From Jesse's Root, and the Peaceable Kingdom
events.detail: A ruler from David's own line, resting on the LORD's Spirit, will judge the poor fairly rather than by appearances, in a renewed world so transformed that wolves lie down with lambs and a child can play safely over a snake's nest.

verses.text: A wolf will reside with a lamb, and a leopard will lie down with a young goat; an ox and a young lion will graze together, as a small child leads them along.
They will no longer injure or destroy on my entire royal mountain. For there will be universal submission to the LORD's [Yahweh's] sovereignty, just as the waters completely cover the sea.

events.title: Israel's Scattered People Gathered Home
events.detail: The root of Jesse becomes a signal flag drawing the nations, and old hostility between Ephraim and Judah finally ends as the LORD gathers his people's dispersed remnant from every corner of the earth.

events.title: A Song of Praise and Deliverance
events.detail: The section that opened with a courtroom lawsuit against Judah closes instead with a short worship song — praise for a God whose anger has subsided into consolation, sung by "citizens of Zion" celebrating that "the Holy One of Israel acts mightily among you."

verses.text: Look, God [El] is my deliverer! I will trust in him and not fear. For the LORD [Yahweh] gives me strength and protects me; he has become my deliverer.

eras.label: Era XI · Isaiah 13
eras.name: Oracle Against Babylon
eras.dates: The first in a long run of oracles against foreign nations opens with the empire that will one day destroy Jerusalem itself — Babylon — pictured as already doomed, its fall described so completely that the chapter promises the city will never be inhabited again.

events.title: The LORD Musters an Army Against Babylon
events.detail: A coming army is summoned from a distant land as the LORD's own instrument of judgment, and "the day of the LORD" is named explicitly for the first time in the book as a day of cruelty that will darken the sun, moon, and stars themselves.

verses.text: Wail, for the LORD's [Yahweh's] day of judgment is near; it comes with all the destructive power of the Sovereign One.

events.title: The Medes, and Babylon's Permanent Desolation
events.detail: The Medes are named as the specific agents of Babylon's fall, and the once-admired capital is left to hyenas, ostriches, and wild goats — never again to be rebuilt or resettled, even by a passing nomad's tent.

eras.label: Era XII · Isaiah 14
eras.name: The Taunt Against the King of Babylon
eras.dates: Israel's coming relief from suffering turns into an extended taunt song mocking Babylon's fallen king, imagined descending to Sheol to be met by the ridicule of dead kings before him — a passage whose language of a "shining one" cast down from the sky has been read at multiple levels throughout history — closing with shorter notes on Assyria's yoke and a warning to Philistia.

events.title: "How You Have Fallen From the Sky, O Shining One"
events.detail: Once Israel finds relief from its oppressor, it will taunt the king of Babylon directly — pictured descending to Sheol to be mocked by the very kings he once conquered, having claimed he would "climb up to the sky" and "make myself like the Most High," only to be thrown out of his own grave like discarded rubbish.

verses.text: "Look how you have fallen from the sky, O shining one, son of the dawn!… I will climb up to the sky. Above the stars of El I will set up my throne… I will make myself like the Most High!"

events.title: Assyria's Yoke Broken, and a Warning to Philistia
events.detail: The LORD reaffirms his settled plan against Assyria with a solemn vow that nothing can frustrate, then turns briefly to warn Philistia not to celebrate one broken enemy, since a worse one — described as a viper's offspring — is still coming.

verses.text: "Be sure of this: Just as I have intended, so it will be; just as I have planned, it will happen."

eras.label: Era XIII · Isaiah 15-16
eras.name: Oracle Against Moab
eras.dates: Moab's cities fall in a single night, sending refugees fleeing with what little they can carry, and a plea to Judah's king for asylum is met with the promise of a future trustworthy ruler from David's line — though Moab's own empty boasting ensures the oracle ends in lament rather than rescue.

events.title: Moab Devastated in a Night
events.detail: Moab's cities are destroyed so suddenly that the whole nation is described in mourning within a single verse-sequence — shaved heads, sackcloth, and refugees fleeing as far as Zoar — with the oracle noting there is worse trouble yet to come.

events.title: A Plea for Refuge, and Moab's Empty Pride
events.detail: Moabite refugees are urged to seek asylum in Judah under a coming trustworthy king from David's line, but Moab's own "great arrogance" and empty boasting mean its wailing over ruined vineyards will not be answered, with the LORD setting an exact three-year timetable on what splendor remains.

verses.text: Then a trustworthy king will be established; he will rule in a reliable manner, this one from David's family. He will be sure to make just decisions and will be experienced in executing justice.

eras.label: Era XIV · Isaiah 17-18
eras.name: Oracle Against Damascus and Ephraim, and Cush
eras.dates: Damascus and Ephraim's northern kingdom fall together as allied powers, reduced to gleaned olive branches and abandoned altars, while a separate short oracle addresses a distant African nation whose messengers will eventually bring tribute to the LORD on Mount Zion.

events.title: Damascus and Ephraim Reduced to Gleanings
events.detail: Syria's capital and Israel's northern kingdom fall together as allied powers, reduced to the handful of olives left after a harvest, with the survivors finally trusting their actual Creator instead of the altars their own hands made.

verses.text: At that time men will trust in their Creator; they will depend on the Holy One of Israel. They will no longer trust in the altars their hands made.

events.title: A Nation Beyond the Rivers of Cush
events.detail: A short, distinctive oracle addresses a tall, feared nation beyond the rivers of Cush, watching from a distance as the LORD acts in his own time, before predicting that this same distant people will one day bring tribute to Mount Zion themselves.

eras.label: Era XV · Isaiah 19-20
eras.name: Oracle Against Egypt, and the Sign of Isaiah's Nakedness
eras.dates: Egypt collapses into civil war and failed sorcery as the Nile itself dries up, yet the oracle ends on a startling reversal — Egypt, Assyria, and Israel worshiping together as equally blessed nations — before Isaiah performs an uncomfortable three-year sign-act, walking stripped and barefoot as a living warning against trusting Egypt for help.

events.title: Egypt's Civil Strife, and a Dried-Up Nile
events.detail: Egypt's idols tremble as the LORD provokes internal conflict, dries up the Nile, and exposes Pharaoh's celebrated wise advisers as fools who "lead Egypt astray in all she does."

events.title: Egypt, Assyria, and Israel Blessed Together
events.detail: In one of the book's most striking reversals, Egypt turns to the LORD, an altar is raised inside Egyptian territory, and the chapter closes with Egypt, Assyria, and Israel named jointly as "my people," "the work of my hands," and "my special possession."

verses.text: "Blessed be my people, Egypt, and the work of my hands, Assyria, and my special possession, Israel!"

events.title: Isaiah Walks Naked and Barefoot
events.detail: As an uncomfortable three-year object lesson, Isaiah walks stripped of sandals and outer clothing to dramatize how Assyria will lead away Egyptian and Cushite captives — a living warning against the very source of hope those watching had counted on.

eras.label: Era XVI · Isaiah 21-22
eras.name: The Fall of Babylon Foreseen, and the Valley of Vision
eras.dates: A guard is posted to watch for Babylon's fall and reports it before it happens, shorter oracles follow concerning Dumah, Arabia, and Kedar, and the section closes in Jerusalem itself — the Valley of Vision — where celebration rather than repentance meets a coming siege, and a proud palace official is deposed to make way for another.

events.title: "Babylon Has Fallen, Fallen!"
events.detail: A watchman posted at Isaiah's own anguished instruction reports the very thing the chapter has been building toward — Babylon's fall and the shattering of her idols — delivered as urgent news to Isaiah's own downtrodden people.

verses.text: "Babylon has fallen, fallen! All the idols of her gods lie shattered on the ground!"

events.title: Oracles Concerning Dumah and Arabia
events.detail: Two brief oracles address Seir and the Arabian caravans of Dedan and Tema, the first ending in an unanswered question about how much of the night remains, the second predicting Kedar's splendor will end within exactly one year.

events.title: The Valley of Vision: Celebration Instead of Repentance
events.detail: Jerusalem's own defensive preparations — inventorying houses, building reservoirs — are condemned for trusting engineering over the God "who formed it long ago," while the city responds to the crisis not with mourning but with feasting: "eat and drink, for tomorrow we die!"

verses.text: The Sovereign LORD [Adonai Yahweh] of Heaven's Armies called for weeping and mourning… But look, there is outright celebration! You say, "Kill the ox and slaughter the sheep, eat meat and drink wine… for tomorrow we die!"

events.title: Shebna Deposed, Eliakim Installed
events.detail: A specific palace official, Shebna, is condemned for carving himself an elevated tomb and stripped of his office, replaced by Eliakim — though even Eliakim's authority is pictured as a peg that will eventually come loose under the weight hung on it.

eras.label: Era XVII · Isaiah 23
eras.name: Oracle Against Tyre
eras.dates: The great maritime trading power of Tyre is humbled along with her sister city Sidon, her commerce silenced for seventy years — a lifetime of a king — before the oracle closes with an unusual promise that Tyre's eventual restored profits will be dedicated to the LORD rather than hoarded.

events.title: Tyre and Sidon's Trade Silenced
events.detail: Word of Tyre's devastation spreads across the Mediterranean trading world it once dominated, its harbor emptied and its dignitaries humiliated, likened at the chapter's end to the already-fallen Chaldeans.

events.title: Tyre Remembered After Seventy Years
events.detail: After seventy years — "the typical life span of a king" — Tyre will resume business like a forgotten prostitute singing for attention again, but this time her profits will be set apart for the LORD rather than stored up for herself.

eras.label: Era XVIII · Isaiah 24
eras.name: The Earth Laid Waste
eras.dates: The scope suddenly widens from individual nations to the entire earth, devastated so completely under a broken "permanent treaty" that every class of person — priest and layperson, master and servant — suffers the same fate, though scattered voices of praise still rise even amid the ruin.

events.title: The Earth Devastated Under a Broken Covenant
events.detail: Unlike the preceding chapters' national oracles, this judgment falls on "the earth" itself without distinction of class or wealth, blamed on a violated "permanent treaty" and pictured through the silencing of every instrument of celebration, down to the last olive left after harvest.

verses.text: The earth is defiled by its inhabitants, for they have violated laws, disregarded the regulation, and broken the permanent treaty.

events.title: Scattered Praise Amid Terror
events.detail: Even amid a judgment where "terror, pit, and snare" await every inhabitant and the earth staggers like a drunk, scattered voices lift up praise from the coastlands, anticipating a day when the LORD will reign in visible splendor on Mount Zion.

eras.label: Era XIX · Isaiah 25-26
eras.name: A Song of Praise, and Trust in the LORD
eras.dates: Isaiah bursts into personal praise for a God who turns fortified cities to rubble and death itself into a swallowed enemy, before a communal song of trust follows — the level path prepared for the righteous, a plea that leans on the promise of bodily resurrection, and a call to hide briefly until judgment passes.

events.title: "He Will Swallow Up Death Permanently"
events.detail: Isaiah's own personal song of praise pictures the LORD hosting a banquet of rich food for all nations on Mount Zion, and declares that death itself — not merely political enemies — will be swallowed up forever, with every tear wiped from every face.

verses.text: he will swallow up death permanently. The Sovereign Lord [Adonai Yahweh] will wipe away the tears from every face, and remove his people's disgrace from all the earth.

events.title: Trust in the LORD, and the Dead Will Live Again
events.detail: A communal song celebrates a "strong city" secured by trust rather than walls, before turning to one of the Old Testament's clearest statements of bodily resurrection — the dead not merely surviving but actually rising to shout for joy.

verses.text: You keep completely safe the people who maintain their faith, for they trust in you. Trust in the LORD [Yahweh] from this time forward.
Your dead will come back to life; your corpses will rise up. Wake up and shout joyfully, you who live in the ground!

events.title: "Hide for a Little While"
events.detail: A brief, urgent instruction closes the song: enter your rooms and shut the door until the LORD's anger has passed, since he is coming out to punish the earth's sin and will no longer hide the blood shed on it.

eras.label: Era XX · Isaiah 27
eras.name: Leviathan Punished, and Israel's Restoration
eras.dates: The LORD's sword finally reaches the sea monster Leviathan itself, the vineyard song from chapter 5 is quietly answered with a vineyard now tenderly guarded rather than judged, and the chapter closes with a great trumpet calling scattered exiles home to worship on the holy mountain.

events.title: Leviathan Punished, and the Vineyard Replanted
events.detail: The chaotic sea monster Leviathan is finally slain by the LORD's own sword, and the vineyard imagery from chapter 5 returns transformed — no longer producing sour grapes under judgment, but guarded night and day so "no one can harm it."

verses.text: "I, the LORD [Yahweh], protect it; I water it regularly. I guard it night and day, so no one can harm it."

events.title: Exiles Gathered Home by a Great Trumpet
events.detail: Jacob's sin is described as forgiven once every idolatrous altar stone is crushed to limestone, and the section on judgment closes on a note of homecoming — a great trumpet sounding to gather the lost from both Assyria and Egypt to worship on Jerusalem's holy mountain.

eras.label: Era XXI · Isaiah 28
eras.name: Woe to Ephraim's Drunkards, and the Cornerstone in Zion
eras.dates: A new cycle of woe oracles opens with Ephraim's leaders too drunk to see straight, even their prophets stumbling over their own visions, before the LORD promises a tested, reliable cornerstone in Zion for anyone willing to trust it rather than a false "treaty with death" — closing with a farmer's parable about purposeful, varied work.

events.title: Ephraim's Drunkards, and Vomit-Covered Tables
events.detail: Ephraim's leadership — priests and prophets alike — is pictured staggering drunk through prophetic visions and legal judgments, their tables covered in vomit, while the LORD's clear message sounds to them like meaningless babble precisely because they refused to listen when it was plain.

verses.text: Even these men stagger because of wine; they stumble around because of beer— priests and prophets stagger because of beer, they are confused because of wine.

events.title: A Tested Cornerstone in Zion
events.detail: Jerusalem's rulers, who boast of a "treaty with death" that will let disaster pass them by, are answered with the promise of a real cornerstone the LORD is laying in Zion — one that will not panic those who trust it, even as the false treaty is dissolved by the very judgment it claimed to escape.

verses.text: "Look, I am laying a stone in Zion, an approved stone, set in place as a precious cornerstone for the foundation. The one who maintains his faith will not panic."

events.title: The Parable of the Farmer
events.detail: A closing parable compares the LORD's varied, purposeful methods of judgment to a farmer who does not plow forever, but times and differentiates his work — plowing, then planting, then threshing each crop by the method suited to it — since "this also comes from the LORD of Heaven's Armies."

eras.label: Era XXII · Isaiah 29
eras.name: Woe to Ariel
eras.dates: Jerusalem itself, called "Ariel" here, is warned it will be besieged and humbled to the point of speaking from the dust — yet the same chapter promises the coming horde will vanish like a bad dream, and that a day is coming when the deaf will hear words from a sealed scroll they currently cannot even have read to them.

events.title: Ariel Besieged, and a Sealed Scroll
events.detail: Jerusalem, addressed by the ancient name "Ariel," is warned of a coming siege severe enough to reduce her voice to a whisper from the dust, while the LORD's revelation becomes like a sealed scroll no one — literate or not — can actually read, since the people's worship has become empty ritual.

verses.text: "These people say they are loyal to me… but they are not really loyal to me. Their worship consists of nothing but man-made ritual."

events.title: The Potter and the Clay
events.detail: Those who think they can hide their plans from the LORD are rebuked with the image of clay questioning its potter, before the chapter turns hopeful — the deaf will hear a scroll's words, the blind will see, and the descendants of Jacob will honor the Holy One of Israel rather than fear shame.

verses.text: "Your thinking is perverse! Should the potter be regarded as clay? Should the thing made say about its maker, 'He didn't make me'?"

eras.label: Era XXIII · Isaiah 30
eras.name: Woe to the Rebellious Children Who Trust Egypt
eras.dates: Judah's leaders are condemned for forming an alliance with Egypt without ever consulting the LORD, a plan the chapter predicts will collapse suddenly like a cracked wall, before it turns to real hope — a patient, gracious LORD waiting to be asked, and a final vision of him arriving in fury to shatter Assyria.

events.title: An Alliance With Egypt, Made Without Consulting the LORD
events.detail: Judah's officials travel to Egypt for military protection without ever asking the LORD's will, a decision condemned as compounding their sin, and pictured collapsing suddenly "like a high wall that bulges and cracks" — shattered so completely no shard remains large enough to scoop a coal from a fire.

verses.text: "The rebellious children are as good as dead," says the LORD, "those who make plans without consulting me, who form alliances without consulting my Spirit."

events.title: "The LORD Is Ready to Show You Mercy"
events.detail: Against the backdrop of rebellion, the LORD is described waiting to be gracious and ready to have compassion, promising that a people who once hid their teachers will finally see them plainly, with light itself multiplied sevenfold when healing finally comes.

verses.text: For this reason the LORD [Yahweh] is ready to show you mercy; he sits on his throne, ready to have compassion on you. Indeed, the LORD [Yahweh] is a just God [Elohim]; all who wait for him in faith will be blessed.

events.title: The LORD's Name Comes in Fury Against Assyria
events.detail: The chapter closes with the LORD himself arriving from a distant place in raging anger, his voice shattering Assyria specifically, in a scene pictured as an already-prepared burial pyre, deep and wide, waiting for a king.

eras.label: Era XXIV · Isaiah 31-32
eras.name: Woe to Those Who Rely on Egypt's Horses, and the Reign of a Righteous King
eras.dates: The chapter renews its warning against trusting Egyptian cavalry over the Holy One of Israel, promising the LORD himself will defend Jerusalem like a lion guarding its prey, before shifting into a vision of ideal government — a king who promotes fairness, officials who tell the truth, and a Spirit poured out that finally settles justice into the land itself.

events.title: "They Do Not Rely on the Holy One of Israel"
events.detail: Those trusting Egypt's chariots and horsemen instead of the LORD are warned plainly that flesh is not spirit, while the LORD promises to defend Jerusalem the way a lion defends its kill or hovering birds protect a nest — fiercely and personally.

verses.text: Those who go down to Egypt for help are as good as dead… But they do not rely on the Holy One of Israel and do not seek help from the LORD [Yahweh].

events.title: A King Who Promotes Fairness
events.detail: In deliberate contrast to the corrupt leadership condemned throughout the preceding chapters, a coming king and his officials are pictured as shelter from storms and shade from heat, giving sight to the blind and understanding to the rash.

events.title: The Spirit Poured Out, and Justice Settled
events.detail: Complacent women are warned that comfortable ease will fail when harvest itself fails, but the chapter turns forward to a time when the Spirit is poured out from heaven, transforming wilderness into fertile orchard and finally letting "justice settle down" to stay.

verses.text: Fairness will produce peace and result in lasting security.

eras.label: Era XXV · Isaiah 33
eras.name: Woe to the Destroyer, and Zion's Security
eras.dates: An unnamed destroyer who has himself never been destroyed is warned his own turn is coming, a communal cry for mercy rises up amid broken treaties and empty highways, and the chapter resolves into a settled, secure Jerusalem where the LORD himself serves as ruler, judge, and king all at once.

events.title: The Destroyer Doomed, and the Land in Mourning
events.detail: An unnamed destroyer — likely Assyria — is warned that the destruction it has dealt out will return to it in kind, while the land itself is pictured withering under broken treaties and despised witnesses, its highways emptied of travelers.

verses.text: The destroyer is as good as dead, you who have not been destroyed!… When you are through destroying, you will be destroyed; when you finish deceiving, others will deceive you!

events.title: "The LORD, Our King — He Will Deliver Us"
events.detail: The LORD rises to exalt himself as the one true refuge for those who live uprightly and refuse bribery, and the chapter closes on a settled, secure Jerusalem — its stakes never pulled up, its ropes never snapped, ruled by the LORD as commander, judge, and king together.

verses.text: For the LORD [Yahweh], our ruler, the LORD [Yahweh], our commander, the LORD [Yahweh], our king— he will deliver us.

eras.label: Era XXVI · Isaiah 34-35
eras.name: Judgment on Edom, and the Highway of Holiness
eras.dates: A day of the LORD's vengeance falls specifically on Edom, its land turned permanently to burning pitch and its ruins given over to owls and jackals — a scene of total desolation deliberately answered by the following chapter's opposite vision: a healed wilderness bursting into bloom, crossed by a safe highway called the Way of Holiness.

events.title: Edom's Land Turned to Burning Pitch
events.detail: The LORD's sword, already described descending on the nations generally, is now aimed specifically at Edom for its hostility toward Zion, turning the land into permanent burning pitch inhabited by owls, jackals, and hawks "through successive generations."

verses.text: For the LORD [Yahweh] has planned a day of revenge, a time when he will repay Edom for her hostility toward Zion.

events.title: The Wilderness Blooms, and the Way of Holiness
events.detail: In deliberate contrast to Edom's ruin, the wilderness itself is promised transformation — blind eyes opened, the lame leaping like deer — crossed by a safe highway called the Way of Holiness, reserved for the ransomed making their happy-shouting way home to Zion.

verses.text: Then blind eyes will open, deaf ears will hear. Then the lame will leap like a deer, the mute tongue will shout for joy.
A thoroughfare will be there— it will be called the Way of Holiness. The unclean will not travel on it.

eras.label: Era XXVII · Isaiah 36
eras.name: Sennacherib's Chief Adviser Taunts Jerusalem
eras.dates: The prophetic oracles give way to historical narrative, matching the account in 2 Kings, as Sennacherib's field commander stands outside Jerusalem's walls and publicly mocks Hezekiah's trust in both Egypt and the LORD, demanding surrender in language deliberately designed to terrify the listening population.

events.title: "What Is Your Source of Confidence?"
events.detail: With Judah's fortified cities already captured, Sennacherib's chief adviser confronts Hezekiah's officials at the very spot Isaiah once met Ahaz, mocking trust in both Egypt's "splintered reed" and the LORD, whose own high places Hezekiah had torn down.

verses.text: "Look, you must be trusting in Egypt, that splintered reed staff. If someone leans on it for support, it punctures his hand and wounds him."

events.title: The Taunt Shouted in Hebrew for All to Hear
events.detail: Deliberately switching from diplomatic Aramaic to the common Hebrew dialect so the watching people on the wall can understand, the chief adviser promises comfortable exile over rescue and asks whether any god of any nation has ever actually rescued its people from Assyria.

verses.text: "Have any of the gods of the nations rescued their lands from the power of the king of Assyria?"

eras.label: Era XXVIII · Isaiah 37
eras.name: Hezekiah's Prayer, and the Angel of the LORD
eras.dates: Hezekiah tears his clothes and takes the threatening letter directly into the temple to spread before the LORD, receiving through Isaiah a detailed answer naming Sennacherib's arrogance and promising rescue — fulfilled overnight when the angel of the LORD strikes down 185,000 Assyrian troops in a single night.

events.title: Hezekiah's Distress, and a Second Threatening Letter
events.detail: Hezekiah responds to the crisis not with counter-threats but with sackcloth and a direct appeal to Isaiah, while Sennacherib sends a second letter designed to make trusting the LORD sound as naive as trusting any other conquered nation's god.

verses.text: "This is a day of distress, insults, and humiliation… Perhaps the LORD [Yahweh] your God will hear all these things… So pray for this remnant that remains."

events.title: Hezekiah's Prayer Spread Before the LORD
events.detail: Hezekiah takes Sennacherib's actual letter into the temple and physically spreads it out before the LORD, praying not primarily for his own safety but "so all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the LORD."

verses.text: "O LORD [Yahweh] of Heaven's Armies, O God [Elohim] of Israel, who is enthroned on the cherubim! You alone are God [Elohim] over all the kingdoms of the earth."

events.title: Sennacherib's Death, and 185,000 Struck Down in a Night
events.detail: Isaiah delivers the LORD's detailed answer — Jerusalem mocks her attacker rather than fearing him, and Sennacherib will be led back the way he came — fulfilled when the angel of the LORD kills 185,000 Assyrian troops overnight, and Sennacherib himself is later assassinated by his own sons while worshiping his god.

verses.text: The angel of the LORD [Yahweh] went out and killed 185,000 troops in the Assyrian camp. When they got up early the next morning, there were all the corpses!

eras.label: Era XXIX · Isaiah 38-39
eras.name: Hezekiah's Illness and Healing, and the Babylonian Envoys
eras.dates: Hezekiah is struck with a terminal illness and pleads for his life, receiving fifteen additional years confirmed by a miraculous sign involving a sundial's shadow, but his subsequent pride in showing Babylonian envoys his entire treasury draws a sobering prophecy of future exile.

events.title: Fifteen Years Added, Confirmed by a Shadow
events.detail: Told plainly he will die, Hezekiah turns his face to the wall and weeps bitterly, and the LORD responds by adding fifteen years to his life, confirmed with an unmistakable sign — the shadow on the palace stairway visibly moving backward ten steps.

verses.text: "Go and tell Hezekiah: 'This is what the LORD [Yahweh] God [Elohim] of your ancestor David says: "I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Look, I will add 15 years to your life."'"

events.title: Hezekiah's Psalm of Recovery
events.detail: Hezekiah's own recorded psalm moves from despair at facing Sheol "in the middle of my life" to gratitude that the living, not the dead, are the ones who can actually praise God — a theology of thanksgiving grounded specifically in still being alive.

verses.text: The living person, the living person, he gives you thanks, as I do today. A father tells his sons about your faithfulness.

events.title: The Babylonian Envoys, and a Warning of Exile
events.detail: Hezekiah proudly shows visiting Babylonian envoys his entire treasury and armory, prompting Isaiah's sober prediction that everything shown off will one day be carried away to Babylon — a warning Hezekiah accepts with troubling relief that at least it will not happen in his own lifetime.

verses.text: "A time is coming when everything in your palace… will be carried away to Babylon; nothing will be left," says the LORD [Yahweh].

eras.label: Era XXX · Isaiah 40
eras.name: "Comfort, Comfort My People" — the Incomparable God
eras.dates: The book's tone shifts decisively at chapter 40, opening not in judgment but in comfort — a voice crying out in the wilderness to prepare the LORD's way — before a sweeping celebration of God's incomparable power over creation closes with the promise that those who wait for him will run without growing weary.

events.title: "Comfort, Comfort My People"
events.detail: After thirty-nine chapters weighted toward judgment, the book pivots decisively: Jerusalem's punishment is declared complete, a voice cries out to prepare a highway for God in the wilderness, and the LORD is pictured tenderly as a shepherd gathering lambs in his arms.

verses.text: "Comfort, comfort my people," says your God… A voice cries out, "In the wilderness clear a way for the LORD [Yahweh]; build a level road through the rift valley for our God [Elohim]."
Like a shepherd he tends his flock; he gathers up the lambs with his arm; he carries them close to his heart.

events.title: Who Has Measured the Waters in His Hand?
events.detail: A cascading series of rhetorical questions establishes God's incomparable scale — nations are like a drop in a bucket to him, idol-makers must search for wood that won't rot just to keep their gods upright, and the stars themselves are called out by name under his command.

verses.text: Look, the nations are like a drop in a bucket; they are regarded as dust on the scales.
To whom can you compare God [El]? To what image can you liken him?

events.title: "Those Who Wait for the LORD Find Renewed Strength"
events.detail: Against Israel's complaint that God is unaware of its troubles, the chapter closes with its most quoted promise — that those who wait on the LORD will rise on wings like eagles, running without growing weary.

verses.text: But those who wait for the LORD's [Yahweh's] help find renewed strength; they rise up as if they had eagles' wings, they run without growing weary, they walk without getting tired.

eras.label: Era XXXI · Isaiah 41
eras.name: Israel My Servant, "Fear Not"
eras.dates: The LORD summons a courtroom-style debate with the nations over who really controls history, singling out a conqueror stirred up from the east, before turning to comfort Israel directly with the book's recurring reassurance — "don't be afraid, I am helping you" — and mocking the idols who cannot even answer when called on.

events.title: A Conqueror Summoned From the East
events.detail: The LORD opens a courtroom-style challenge to the nations, asking who has stirred up a conqueror from the east who tramples kings like dust — a question the terrified coastlands answer only by huddling together to encourage one another and nail their idols down more securely.

events.title: "Don't Be Afraid, for I Am With You"
events.detail: Israel is addressed directly and tenderly as "my servant," the offspring of Abraham my friend, promised that the LORD himself takes hold of its right hand — a promise extended concretely into streams flowing in the wilderness and trees growing in the desert.

verses.text: "Don't be afraid, for I am with you! Don't be frightened, for I am your God [Elohim]! I strengthen you— yes, I help you— yes, I uphold you with my victorious right hand!"

events.title: A Courtroom Challenge to the Idols
events.detail: The LORD challenges the idols to predict anything at all, past or future, good or bad, and declares the verdict already in: they are nothing, their accomplishments nonexistent, and not one of them ever announced anything true in advance.

verses.text: Look, you are nothing, and your accomplishments are nonexistent; the one who chooses to worship you is disgusting.

eras.label: Era XXXII · Isaiah 42
eras.name: The Servant Who Brings Justice, and Israel's Blind Deafness
eras.dates: The first of the book's four "Servant Songs" introduces a figure who will bring justice to the nations not through shouting but through gentleness toward the weak, followed by a hymn of praise and a jarring reversal — Israel itself called blind and deaf, plundered precisely because it would not listen to the LORD's own law.

events.title: The Servant Who Will Not Break a Crushed Reed
events.detail: In language later applied directly to Jesus in the Gospels, the LORD introduces "my servant" — chosen, Spirit-empowered, and characterized by gentleness rather than force, who will not break a bruised reed or snuff out a dim wick on his way to establishing justice.

verses.text: "Here is my servant whom I support, my chosen one in whom I take pleasure. I have placed my Spirit on him; he will make just decrees for the nations… A crushed reed he will not break, a dim wick he will not extinguish."

events.title: A New Song, and the LORD as Warrior
events.detail: A fresh song of praise calls the coastlands and the whole earth to sing, before the LORD is pictured shifting suddenly from silence into the active posture of a warrior rousing himself for battle.

events.title: Israel, the Blind and Deaf Servant
events.detail: In a sharp reversal, Israel itself — not merely the nations — is called "blind" and "deaf," plundered and looted precisely because it refused to follow the LORD's law, a judgment the people did not even recognize while it was happening.

verses.text: "Who is blind but my servant? Who is deaf like my messenger I sent?"

eras.label: Era XXXIII · Isaiah 43
eras.name: "When You Pass Through the Waters, I Am With You"
eras.dates: A tender promise of protection through disaster — water, fire, and exile all named directly — grounds itself in Israel's identity as a people created specifically for the LORD's own glory, before the chapter turns to a striking accusation: Israel never truly burdened itself with worship in the first place, yet the LORD blots out its sins anyway, for his own sake.

events.title: "When You Pass Through the Waters, I Am With You"
events.detail: One of the book's most personal promises assures Israel that water will not overwhelm it and fire will not burn it, because it is precious, loved, and created specifically "for my glory" — a promise reinforced by naming Israel as the LORD's own witnesses that no other god was formed before him.

verses.text: "When you pass through the waters, I am with you; when you pass through the streams, they will not overwhelm you. When you walk through the fire, you will not be burned."
"You are my witnesses," says the LORD [Yahweh], "my servant whom I have chosen so that you may consider and believe in me, and understand that I am he."

events.title: "I Am About to Do Something New"
events.detail: The LORD who once made a road through the sea at the exodus now promises something genuinely new — a road through the wilderness and streams in the wasteland — explicitly asking Israel to stop dwelling on former things in favor of what is about to happen.

verses.text: "Look, I am about to do something new. Now it begins to happen! Do you not recognize it? Yes, I will make a road in the wilderness and paths in the wastelands."

events.title: "I Blot Out Your Rebellious Deeds for My Own Sake"
events.detail: In a striking accusation, the LORD notes that Israel never actually burdened itself with the sacrifices it claims to have offered — yet declares he blots out its rebellious deeds anyway, entirely for his own sake rather than because of anything Israel has done to deserve it.

verses.text: "I, I am the one who blots out your rebellious deeds for my sake; your sins I do not remember."

eras.label: Era XXXIV · Isaiah 44
eras.name: The Folly of Idol-Making, and Cyrus Named by Name
eras.dates: One of the Bible's most extended satires of idolatry describes a craftsman burning half a log for warmth and cooking, then carving the other half into a god he prays to for rescue, before the chapter closes on a specific and startling prophecy — a foreign king named Cyrus, called by name more than a century before his birth, appointed as the LORD's own shepherd to rebuild Jerusalem.

events.title: "I Am the First and I Am the Last"
events.detail: Israel, formed in the womb and helped by the LORD from birth, is told not to panic, since there is no other sheltering rock the LORD knows of — a claim to absolute uniqueness that frames the idol satire immediately following.

verses.text: "I am the first and I am the last, there is no God [Elohim] but me."

events.title: The Craftsman Who Burns Half a Log and Worships the Other Half
events.detail: In the book's most extended satire of idol-making, a craftsman is shown using half of a felled tree to warm himself and bake bread, then carving the remaining half into a god he bows down to and prays to for rescue — never once stopping to notice the absurdity of what he has done.

verses.text: No one thinks to himself… "I burned half of it in the fire… With the rest of it should I make a disgusting idol? Should I bow down to dry wood?"

events.title: Cyrus Named by Name
events.detail: The chapter closes with one of the book's most specific predictive claims — a Persian king named Cyrus, more than a century before his birth, named outright as the shepherd the LORD will use to decree Jerusalem's rebuilding and the temple's reconstruction.

verses.text: "who commissions Cyrus, the one I appointed as shepherd to carry out all my wishes and to decree concerning Jerusalem, 'She will be rebuilt,' and concerning the temple, 'It will be reconstructed.'"

eras.label: Era XXXV · Isaiah 45
eras.name: Cyrus, the LORD's Anointed — Though He Does Not Know Him
eras.dates: The LORD directly addresses Cyrus as his chosen instrument, remarkably noting the Persian king does not even recognize the God commissioning him, before the chapter turns to defend the LORD's right to work through unlikely means and closes with a universal invitation extending all the way to the earth's most remote regions.

events.title: "Cyrus, Whose Right Hand I Hold"
events.detail: The LORD speaks directly to Cyrus as his "chosen one," promising to level mountains and shatter bronze doors before him — remarkable not only for naming a pagan king this specifically but for stating twice that Cyrus does this "even though you do not submit to me" and "even though you do not recognize me."

verses.text: "For the sake of my servant Jacob, Israel, my chosen one, I call you by name… I am the LORD [Yahweh], I have no peer, there is no God [Elohim] but me. I arm you for battle, even though you do not recognize me."

events.title: The Potter and the Clay, Again
events.detail: Anyone who questions the LORD's methods is compared again to clay arguing with its potter, before the chapter insists God did not create the earth "without order" or leave it a wasteland — he formed it specifically to be inhabited, and speaks openly rather than in secret riddles.

verses.text: "I am the LORD [Yahweh], I have no peer… he established it, he did not create it without order, he formed it to be inhabited."

events.title: "Every Knee Will Bow to Me"
events.detail: A universal invitation reaches all the way to the earth's remote regions, closing on a solemn oath — the language Paul later echoes in Philippians — that every knee will bow and every tongue affirm the LORD's power to deliver.

verses.text: "Turn to me so you can be delivered, all you who live in the earth's remote regions!… Surely every knee will bow to me, every tongue will solemnly affirm."

eras.label: Era XXXVI · Isaiah 46-47
eras.name: Bel and Nebo Bow Down, and the Fall of Virgin Babylon
eras.dates: Babylon's own gods are pictured as dead weight loaded onto exhausted pack animals, unable even to save themselves from captivity, while the LORD who has carried Israel since birth contrasts himself directly with idols that must be carried — before the section turns to Babylon's own coming humiliation, stripped of her royal pretensions and her trusted magic alike.

events.title: Bel and Nebo Bow Down, but the LORD Carries His People
events.detail: Babylon's own gods, Bel and Nebo, are pictured as dead weight loaded onto tired pack animals headed into captivity themselves, deliberately contrasted with the LORD, who has carried Israel "from birth" and will keep carrying it into old age rather than needing to be carried.

verses.text: "Even when you are old, I will take care of you, even when you have gray hair, I will carry you. I made you and I will support you; I will carry you and rescue you."

events.title: Virgin Daughter Babylon Brought Down
events.detail: Babylon, addressed sarcastically as a pampered "virgin daughter" who called herself eternal and unshakeable, is told to sit in the dirt and grind flour like a slave, her many incantations and astrologers powerless to save her from a disaster arriving "suddenly, in one day."

verses.text: "I am unique! No one can compare to me! I will never have to live as a widow… Both of these will come upon you suddenly, in one day!"

eras.label: Era XXXVII · Isaiah 48
eras.name: "I Am the LORD Your God, Who Teaches You to Succeed"
eras.dates: Stubborn, deceitful Israel is confronted with proof its history was predicted in advance precisely so it could never credit an idol, refined not for its own destruction but "in the furnace of misery," before the chapter closes with an urgent call to leave Babylon behind entirely and a sobering final note: no prosperity for the wicked.

events.title: Refined in the Furnace of Misery
events.detail: Israel's stubbornness — "your neck muscles are like iron" — is met with the LORD's own explanation for predicting events in advance: so no one could ever credit an idol with what only he accomplished, and so his own reputation, not Israel's merit, remains the reason for mercy.

verses.text: "Look, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have purified you in the furnace of misery."

events.title: "Leave Babylon! Flee From the Babylonians!"
events.detail: An urgent evacuation order closes the chapter — leave Babylon and proclaim it joyfully — paired with a wistful "if only" over the prosperity Israel forfeited by disobedience, and a blunt closing verdict allowing no prosperity at all for the wicked.

verses.text: "There will be no prosperity for the wicked," says the LORD [Yahweh].

eras.label: Era XXXVIII · Isaiah 49
eras.name: The Servant's Commission, and "Can a Mother Forget Her Child?"
eras.dates: The second Servant Song describes a figure formed from birth for a mission that at first feels like wasted effort, expanded into a light for the nations reaching to the ends of the earth, before the chapter turns to one of Scripture's most tender images of divine memory — Zion's name inscribed permanently on the LORD's own palms.

events.title: "I Will Make You a Light to the Nations"
events.detail: The Servant describes being formed and commissioned from the womb, admitting a moment of discouragement — "I have worked in vain" — before the LORD expands the mission far beyond restoring Israel alone: "I will make you a light to the nations, so you can bring my deliverance to the remote regions of the earth."

verses.text: "Is it too insignificant a task for you to be my servant… I will make you a light to the nations, so you can bring my deliverance to the remote regions of the earth."

events.title: "Can a Woman Forget Her Nursing Child?"
events.detail: Zion's complaint that the LORD has forgotten her is answered with one of Scripture's most tender images — even if a mother could forget her own nursing child, the LORD could never forget Zion, whose name he has inscribed permanently on the palms of his hands.

verses.text: "Can a woman forget her baby who nurses at her breast?… Even if mothers were to forget, I could never forget you! Look, I have inscribed your name on my palms."

eras.label: Era XXXIX · Isaiah 50
eras.name: The Servant's Obedience Under Suffering
eras.dates: A short but pivotal chapter has the Servant describe absorbing physical abuse without resistance, confident in vindication from the one who helps him — a portrait of obedient suffering that directly anticipates the far more extended suffering of chapter 53.

events.title: "I Did Not Hide My Face From Insults and Spitting"
events.detail: The Servant describes offering his back to those who struck him and his face to those who tore out his beard without resistance, trusting entirely in the Sovereign LORD's help and vindication rather than his own defense — a direct preview of the far fuller suffering portrait still to come in chapter 53.

verses.text: "I offered my back to those who attacked, my jaws to those who tore out my beard; I did not hide my face from insults and spitting. But the Sovereign LORD [Adonai Yahweh] helps me, so I am not humiliated."

eras.label: Era XL · Isaiah 51
eras.name: "Look to the Rock From Which You Were Hewn"
eras.dates: Israel is told to remember its own origin story — a childless Abraham blessed into countless descendants — as grounds for present hope, before the chapter calls on the LORD's own arm to "wake up" the way it once did at the exodus, and closes with the promise that the cup of divine wrath currently being drunk will finally be taken away.

events.title: Look to Abraham and Sarah
events.detail: Those pursuing righteousness are told to look back at their own origin — a single, elderly, childless couple blessed into a multitude — as proof that present desolation is not the final word, since the LORD's deliverance, unlike the fading sky and wearing-out earth, will never disappear.

verses.text: "Look at Abraham, your father, and Sarah, who gave you birth. When I summoned him, he was a lone individual, but I blessed him and gave him numerous descendants."

events.title: "Wake Up, O Arm of the LORD!"
events.detail: A cry for the LORD's own arm to "wake up" as it once did at the exodus recalls the sea monster crushed and the sea dried up as a path for the ransomed, grounding present hope directly in that ancient act of deliverance.

verses.text: "Wake up! Wake up! Clothe yourself with strength, O arm of the LORD [Yahweh]!… Did you not dry up the sea, the waters of the great deep? Did you not make a path through the depths of the sea?"

events.title: The Cup of Wrath Removed
events.detail: Jerusalem, described as having drained a cup of the LORD's anger to its dregs with no one to console her, is promised that same cup will be taken from her hand and placed instead into the hands of her tormentors.

verses.text: "Look, I have removed from your hand the cup of intoxicating wine, the goblet full of my anger. You will no longer have to drink it."

eras.label: Era XLI · Isaiah 52
eras.name: "Awake, Awake, Zion!" — and the Servant Who Will Be Exalted
eras.dates: Zion is called to wake up and shake off the dust of captivity, a messenger's arriving feet are celebrated as beautiful for the good news they carry, and the chapter closes on the brief but startling introduction to the fourth Servant Song — a servant who will be exalted, though first disfigured beyond recognition.

events.title: "Wake Up, Wake Up, Clothe Yourself With Strength, O Zion!"
events.detail: Captive Jerusalem is called to shake off the dust and remove her chains, told plainly that she was "sold for nothing" and therefore "will not be redeemed for money" — a purely gracious rescue rather than a transaction.

events.title: "How Beautiful Are the Feet of the Messenger"
events.detail: One of the book's most quoted lines celebrates the arrival of a messenger bringing good news of peace and deliverance, watched for eagerly by Jerusalem's own watchmen who shout for joy the moment they see the LORD's own return to Zion.

verses.text: How delightful it is to see approaching over the mountains the feet of a messenger who announces peace, a messenger who brings good news.

events.title: The Servant Introduced: Exalted, Though Disfigured
events.detail: In three brief but pivotal verses, the fourth and final Servant Song opens — the servant will be "elevated, lifted high, and greatly exalted," yet the same figure was so disfigured he "no longer looked human," a paradox chapter 53 exists entirely to explain.

verses.text: he was so disfigured he no longer looked like a man; his form was so marred he no longer looked human— so now he will startle many nations.

eras.label: Era XLII · Isaiah 53
eras.name: "He Was Wounded for Our Transgressions" — the Suffering Servant
eras.dates: The book's single most theologically weighted chapter describes a servant despised, rejected, and silent before his accusers, who carries suffering that belongs to others rather than himself — pierced for their rebellion, crushed for their sins, and vindicated afterward for having borne the sin of many.

events.title: "He Was Wounded Because of Our Rebellious Deeds"
events.detail: A figure with no stately form or majesty to attract attention is described as despised and rejected, carrying pain and illness that were never his own — the chapter's central claim stated outright: "the LORD caused the sin of all of us to attack him."

verses.text: But he lifted up our illnesses, he carried our pain… He was wounded because of our rebellious deeds, crushed because of our sins… All of us had wandered off like sheep… but the LORD [Yahweh] caused the sin of all of us to attack him.

events.title: "Like a Lamb Led to the Slaughter"
events.detail: Silent before an unjust trial, buried among the rich despite dying among criminals, the servant's death is described as the LORD's own deliberate purpose, resolved afterward into vindication — he will "see descendants," be "satisfied," and "divide the spoils" for having borne the sin of many.

verses.text: He was treated harshly and afflicted, but he did not even open his mouth. Like a lamb led to the slaughtering block, like a sheep silent before her shearers, he did not even open his mouth.
"My servant will acquit many, for he carried their sins."… he willingly submitted to death and was numbered with the rebels, when he lifted up the sin of many and intervened on behalf of the rebels.

eras.label: Era XLIII · Isaiah 54-55
eras.name: The Barren Woman Sings, and an Everlasting Covenant Offered Freely
eras.dates: Zion, pictured as a formerly barren, abandoned wife, is promised more children than she can house and an unbreakable covenant of peace built on gemstone foundations, before the book's mid-section closes with its own open invitation — free water and wine for anyone thirsty enough to come, since God's ways run as far above human ways as the heavens stand above the earth.

events.title: "Shout for Joy, O Barren One!"
events.detail: Zion, addressed as a formerly barren and briefly abandoned wife, is told to enlarge her tent for more children than she can currently house, grounded in a covenant compared explicitly to the LORD's ancient promise never again to flood the whole earth as in Noah's day.

verses.text: "As far as I am concerned, this is like in Noah's time, when I vowed that the waters of Noah's flood would never again cover the earth… my devotion will not be removed from you."

events.title: "No Weapon Formed Against You Will Succeed"
events.detail: Jerusalem's coming walls and foundations are pictured built from gemstones — antimony, lapis lazuli, beryl — with a promise that closes the chapter on a note quoted often since: no weapon forged against the LORD's servants will ultimately succeed.

verses.text: "No weapon forged to be used against you will succeed; you will refute everyone who tries to accuse you. This is what the LORD [Yahweh] will do for his servants— I will vindicate them," says the LORD [Yahweh].

events.title: "Come to the Water, All Who Are Thirsty"
events.detail: An open invitation to free water and wine closes this half of the book, grounded in the claim that the LORD's thoughts and ways stand as far above human thoughts as the sky stands above the earth, and that his word, like rain, never returns without accomplishing what it was sent to do.

verses.text: "my thoughts are not like your thoughts… for just as the sky is higher than the earth, so my deeds are superior to your deeds and my plans superior to your plans."
"Hey, all who are thirsty, come to the water! You who have no money, come! Buy and eat!"

eras.label: Era XLIV · Isaiah 56-57
eras.name: Foreigners and Eunuchs Welcomed, Blind Watchmen, and Idolatry Denounced
eras.dates: The final section of the book opens by widening the community of worship to include foreigners and eunuchs once excluded, then sharply contrasts that welcome with Israel's own negligent leaders — blind watchmen and greedy "shepherds" — before turning to a direct denunciation of child sacrifice and idolatry practiced under every green tree.

events.title: "My Temple Will Be Known as a Temple for All Nations"
events.detail: Foreigners and eunuchs who keep the Sabbath and hold fast to the covenant are promised full inclusion in the LORD's house of prayer, receiving a monument "better than sons and daughters" — a deliberate widening of who belongs in worship.

verses.text: "I will bring them to my holy mountain; I will make them happy in the temple where people pray to me… my temple will be known as a temple where all nations may pray."

events.title: Blind Watchmen and Mute Dogs
events.detail: Israel's own leaders are condemned in blunt animal imagery — watchmen who are blind, dogs too lazy to bark, shepherds with no understanding who each look out only for their own gain.

events.title: Idolatry Under Every Green Tree
events.detail: The godly are noted to perish without anyone caring, while the nation is accused of child sacrifice "near the streams under the rocky overhangs" and diplomatic missions sent as far as Sheol itself to secure foreign alliances and foreign gods alike.

verses.text: "you who inflame your lusts among the oaks and under every green tree, who slaughter children near the streams under the rocky overhangs."

events.title: "I Dwell With the Humiliated and the Discouraged"
events.detail: The section closes on unexpected tenderness — the high and exalted one who inhabits eternity also dwells specifically with the discouraged and humiliated in order to revive them — though the chapter's very last line still denies peace to the wicked.

verses.text: "I dwell in an exalted and holy place, but also with the discouraged and humiliated, in order to cheer up the humiliated and to encourage the discouraged."

eras.label: Era XLV · Isaiah 58-59
eras.name: True Fasting, and a Confession of Sin
eras.dates: The people's ritual fasting is contrasted sharply with the fasting the LORD actually wants — breaking oppressive yokes and feeding the hungry — before the following chapter turns to an unusually direct national confession of sin, resolved when the LORD himself, seeing no human advocate, takes up justice as his own armor.

events.title: The Fasting the LORD Rejects
events.detail: The people complain their fasting goes unnoticed, but the LORD answers bluntly that a fast accompanied by exploiting workers and picking fights is not the kind of humbling he ever asked for.

events.title: The Fasting the LORD Wants
events.detail: Genuine fasting is redefined entirely in terms of action toward others — loosing chains, sharing food, clothing the naked, honoring the Sabbath — with the promise that light will then break out like the sunrise and ancient ruins will finally be rebuilt.

verses.text: "this is the kind of fast I want: I want you to remove the sinful chains, to tear away the ropes of the burdensome yoke, to set free the oppressed… I want you to share your food with the hungry."

events.title: "Your Sins Have Caused Him to Reject You"
events.detail: The LORD's inability to help is flatly denied — his hand is not too weak, his ear not too deaf — the actual barrier named as sin itself, described through hands stained with blood and lips that speak lies.

verses.text: Look, the LORD's [Yahweh's] hand is not too weak to deliver you… But your sinful acts have alienated you from your God.

events.title: A Confession of Sin, and the LORD Takes Up Justice Himself
events.detail: An unusually direct national confession — "we are aware of our rebellious deeds" — gives way to the LORD seeing no human advocate willing to intervene, so he takes matters into his own hands, arriving as a warrior wearing justice like armor to defend Zion himself.

verses.text: He sees there is no advocate; he is shocked that no one intervenes. So he takes matters into his own hands… He wears his desire for justice like body armor.

eras.label: Era XLVI · Isaiah 60
eras.name: "Arise, Shine!" — Zion's Coming Glory
eras.dates: Zion is called to rise and shine as the LORD's own splendor breaks over her, drawing camel caravans, foreign kings, and the wealth of nations from every direction — a vision of restoration so complete that even the sun and moon become unnecessary once the LORD himself becomes Zion's permanent light.

events.title: "Arise, Shine! For Your Light Arrives!"
events.detail: Zion is called up out of darkness into the LORD's own splendor, drawing nations, kings, and camel caravans loaded with gold and incense from as far away as Sheba and Midian.

verses.text: "Arise! Shine! For your light arrives! The splendor of the LORD [Yahweh] shines on you!"

events.title: The LORD Becomes Zion's Permanent Light
events.detail: Foreigners rebuild Zion's walls and former oppressors bow at her feet, and the vision escalates until it no longer needs the sun or moon at all, since "the LORD will be your permanent source of light" and even the smallest of her people will multiply into a great nation.

verses.text: "The sun will no longer supply light for you by day… the LORD [Yahweh] will be your permanent source of light… your time of sorrow will be over."

eras.label: Era XLVII · Isaiah 61-62
eras.name: "The Spirit of the Sovereign LORD Is Upon Me", and Zion's New Name
eras.dates: A prophetic figure announces a mission of good news to the poor and freedom for captives — the very words Jesus later reads aloud in the Nazareth synagogue — before the following chapter renames Zion entirely, from "Abandoned" and "Desolate" to "My Delight Is in Her," watched over by tireless praying watchmen until the promise is fulfilled.

events.title: "He Has Sent Me to Bind Up the Brokenhearted"
events.detail: A Spirit-anointed figure announces a mission that Jesus will later read aloud verbatim in the Nazareth synagogue and declare fulfilled that day — good news for the poor, freedom for captives, and a turban of joy replacing ashes of mourning.

verses.text: "The Spirit of the Sovereign LORD [Adonai Yahweh] is upon me, because the LORD [Yahweh] has chosen me. He has commissioned me to encourage the poor, to help the brokenhearted, to decree the release of captives."

events.title: Zion Renamed, and Watchmen Who Never Rest
events.detail: Zion is promised an entirely new name reflecting restored status — no longer "Abandoned" but "My Delight Is in Her" — watched over by praying watchmen instructed never to give the LORD rest until Jerusalem's restoration is complete.

verses.text: "You will no longer be called, 'Abandoned,' and your land will no longer be called 'Desolate.' Indeed, you will be called 'My Delight is in Her' and your land 'Married.'"

eras.label: Era XLVIII · Isaiah 63
eras.name: The Divine Warrior From Edom, and a Plea Remembering the Exodus
eras.dates: A striking, blood-soaked vision pictures the LORD returning alone from trampling judgment on Edom like grapes in a winepress, before the tone shifts entirely into a communal recollection of the LORD's ancient faithfulness during the exodus, closing on a raw, unresolved question about why he seems to have let his people go astray. (This chapter's final half-verse is numbered as the opening of chapter 64 in most English translations.)

events.title: "Who Is This Who Comes From Edom, Dressed in Bright Red?"
events.detail: A solitary, blood-stained figure returns from trampling judgment on Edom alone, his garments splashed with the very blood of a winepress metaphor for the nations he has crushed in his own anger "because there was no one to help."

verses.text: "I have stomped grapes in the winepress all by myself; no one from the nations joined me. I stomped on them in my anger; I trampled them down in my rage."

events.title: Remembering the Exodus, and a Raw Plea
events.detail: A communal recollection of the LORD's ancient compassion — lifting and carrying his people "throughout ancient times" — turns into a raw, unresolved question about why he seems to have let them wander from his ways, closing this section on unfinished tension rather than a settled answer.

verses.text: "Why, LORD [Yahweh], do you make us stray from your ways and make our minds stubborn so that we do not obey you? Return for the sake of your servants."

eras.label: Era XLIX · Isaiah 64
eras.name: "If Only You Would Tear Open the Heavens"
eras.dates: The plea left unresolved at the end of chapter 63 continues directly into an urgent cry for the LORD to intervene visibly as he once did, before resolving into one of Scripture's most quoted images of human dependence — clay in the hands of its potter — set against the devastating backdrop of a burned temple. (Its opening half-verse is numbered as the close of chapter 63 in most English translations.)

events.title: "If Only You Would Tear Apart the Sky and Come Down!"
events.detail: The unresolved plea from the previous chapter erupts into an urgent cry for visible divine intervention — mountains trembling, adversaries put on notice — grounded in the claim that no one has ever seen or heard of a God like this who "intervenes for those who wait for him."
