verses.text: If only you would tear apart the sky and come down! The mountains would tremble before you!
Since ancient times no one has heard or perceived, no eye has seen any God besides you, who intervenes for those who wait for him.

events.title: "We Are the Clay, and You Are Our Potter"
events.detail: Confessing that even the nation's "so-called righteous acts" are stained, the plea resolves into a humble image of complete dependence — clay in the hands of its potter — voiced against the devastating backdrop of a burned temple, once the ancestors' pride and joy.

verses.text: Yet, LORD [Yahweh], you are our father. We are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the product of your labor.

eras.label: Era L · Isaiah 65
eras.name: New Heavens, New Earth, and a Reply to False Worship
eras.dates: The LORD answers the preceding lament directly — he was available all along to a people who never sought him — before drawing a sharp line between those who abandon him for feast-gods named Fortune and Destiny and the faithful remnant kept "for the sake of my servants," resolving in one of the book's grandest promises: an entirely new creation without infant death or unfulfilled labor.

events.title: "I Made Myself Available to Those Who Did Not Ask for Me"
events.detail: The LORD answers the plea of the previous chapters directly — he was reaching out all along to a nation that never actually sought him, a people who instead offend him openly with sacrifices in sacred orchards and forbidden foods.

verses.text: "I made myself available to those who did not ask for me; I appeared to those who did not look for me… I spread out my hands all day long to my rebellious people."

events.title: A Remnant Preserved "For the Sake of My Servants"
events.detail: Using the image of good juice found in a damaged grape cluster, the LORD promises not to destroy everyone, preserving a faithful remnant even as those who abandoned him for the gods "Fortune" and "Destiny" are told plainly they will hunger while the LORD's servants feast.

verses.text: "When juice is discovered in a cluster of grapes, someone says, 'Don't destroy it, for it contains juice.' So I will do for the sake of my servants— I will not destroy everyone."

events.title: "I Am About to Create New Heavens and a New Earth"
events.detail: One of the book's grandest promises closes the chapter — an entirely new creation where weeping is never heard again, no infant dies in its first days, and the peaceable-kingdom imagery from chapter 11 returns almost word for word, with the wolf and the lamb grazing together at last.

verses.text: "For look, I am ready to create new heavens and a new earth! The former ones will not be remembered; no one will think about them anymore."
A wolf and a lamb will graze together; a lion, like an ox, will eat straw, and a snake's food will be dirt. They will no longer injure or destroy on my entire royal mountain.

eras.label: Era LI · Isaiah 66
eras.name: Final Judgment, and the New Creation
eras.dates: The book's final chapter contrasts empty temple ritual mixed with abomination against a God who values the humble and contrite, pictures Zion giving birth to a nation in a single astonishing day, and closes on two starkly different endings held side by side — worship gathered from every nation, and an unforgettable, unending image of judgment for those who rebelled.

events.title: "Where Is the House You Will Build for Me?"
events.detail: The LORD, whose throne is the heavens and footstool the earth, questions the very idea of a house built for him, favoring instead the humble and contrite — while condemning worshipers who mix legitimate offerings with practices as abhorrent as human sacrifice.

verses.text: "My hand made them; that is how they came to be," says the LORD [Yahweh]. "I show special favor to the humble and contrite, who respect what I have to say."

events.title: Zion Gives Birth to a Nation in a Single Day
events.detail: In an image without precedent, Zion is pictured going into labor and delivering a full nation before her contractions even properly begin — an unprecedented birth answered by an invitation to nurse and be comforted at her "satisfying breasts" like a child.

verses.text: "Who has ever heard of such a thing? Who has ever seen this? Can a country be brought forth in one day? Can a nation be born in a single moment? Yet as soon as Zion goes into labor she gives birth to sons!"

events.title: The Book's Closing Image: Worship Gathered, Judgment Unending
events.detail: The LORD comes in fire to judge all humanity while simultaneously gathering worshipers "from one Sabbath to the next" from every nation — and the book deliberately ends not on that note of gathered worship but on its stark opposite: an image of undying judgment for the rebellious that later New Testament writers draw on directly.

verses.text: "From one month to the next and from one Sabbath to the next, all people will come to worship me," says the LORD [Yahweh]. "They will go out and observe the corpses of those who rebelled against me, for the maggots that eat them will not die, and the fire that consumes them will not die out."
